title: How I Learned to Love the Conference Racket
author: Phil Dituri
summary: Phil Dituri, a mathematics educator who has attended conferences for almost twenty years and presented more than fifty times, begins by admitting that as a teacher he thought conferences were a racket, since teachers pay dues and fees and even presenters often pay to attend. Having just returned from the NCTM annual meeting in Denver, he offers practical advice on getting real value from such an event. He recommends building a schedule by presenter first and topic second, staying flexible and walking out of sessions that are not useful, and prioritizing conversations over sessions. He also stresses having a workable system for collecting contacts and following up within a week. Lighter advice covers hunting for the best swag as a way to survey the exhibitor hall, taking breaks, asking locals about food, packing snacks, staying at the conference hotel and booking early. The post is an informal, experience-based guide to professional development for teachers, offered as a first draft to be revised.
points: Dituri advises choosing sessions by who is presenting rather than the description, listing every session from people you respect, and then picking one per time slot.
Treat the schedule as a tool rather than an obligation: conferences take no attendance, so leaving an unhelpful session costs nothing.
He argues that connections are the real point of a conference and that a good conversation outranks a session.
Value comes from follow-up, so he suggests reaching out within the following week and keeping contacts in a system you will actually use.
Practical logistics such as breaks, packed snacks, staying at the conference hotel and booking early protect the energy needed to learn.
quotes: As a teacher, I sometimes felt like conferences were a racket. Becoming a teacher generally requires a great deal of education and time. Unlike many other professions requiring higher education, teachers are not known for being paid a particularly high wage to compensate for this extra education
Unless you’re attending with a singular focus, the presenter matters much more than the topic. This is also good advice for registering for college classes: the professor matters more than the class.

Conferences aren’t school. They don’t take attendance. You don’t get credit for completing a session. The only things you’ll take from the conference are a subset of the things you found valuable (and maybe some swag, but more on that later).
Don’t waste any time in sessions you don’t find valuable. Get up and walk out. You’re not offending anyone.
You really don’t have to go to any sessions. They are the pretense for the conference. That conversation you’re excited about, that you’re having, that’s the reason we go to conferences.

It’s much easier to make a great connection and never follow up on it than it is to maintain or cultivate it. Spend just a few minutes reaching out to the people you connected with at some point during the following week.
I have a hard time motivating myself to go “learn about all the products, publishers, and not-for-profits in the space,” so instead I look for the best swag and learn about them in the process.
Take a break. Go outside and take a walk. Skip a session and have a sit-down meal. Leave the conference center to get a tea and take some notes to reflect on what you’ve learned.
